title: "Optimal biomass-based climate change mitigation pathways are spatially heterogeneous due to localized technoeconomic and biophysical constraints"
date: last-modified
abstract: |
  The use of biomass for climate change mitigation offers substantial technical potential, but optimal deployment is highly dependent on spatial, technoeconomic, and biophysical constraints. Blanket climate policies frequently fail to capture this heterogeneity. Here we apply a spatially explicit techno-economic and consequential life cycle assessment framework deployed at a 0.1-degree resolution across the United States, Europe, India, and China. We evaluate the economic viability and carbon abatement potential of three distinct biomass utilization pathways: Bioenergy (BES), Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS), and Bioenergy with Biochar Carbon Storage (BEBCS). Localized constraints, such as distance to geological CO~2~ sinks, baseline grid carbon intensity, and native soil cation exchange capacity, dictate the economically optimal pathway. Traditional BES tends to dominate at low carbon prices, particularly in regions with high wholesale energy prices like Europe, or high grid carbon intensities like India. Biochar (BEBCS) emerges as a highly competitive transition technology at moderate carbon prices, and serves as the optimal long-term pathway in specific agro-ecological zones with degraded soils, such as southern China. Conversely, high capital costs and piecewise long-distance pipeline penalties act as severe barriers to BECCS, which only achieves universal dominance at high carbon prices (e.g., $150/tCO~2~e) where carbon capture revenues finally overwhelm infrastructure penalties. Ultimately, effective climate mitigation requires localized policies that match biomass resources to their most efficient regional end-use.

# Introduction

Biochar has been widely promoted for climate change mitigation, with co-benefits for soil health and crop production when used as a soil amendment.[@woolf2010; @lehmann2021biochar] Globally, biochar has the sustainable technical potential for carbon sequestration and emissions reductions of up to 3.4–6.3 Pg CO~2~e. However, the costs, benefits and tradeoffs for biochar vary spatially, creating substantial heterogeneity in its feasibility at a given carbon price. This variability is further affected by the fact that biochar must compete with alternative uses for the limited supply of available waste biomass. Indeed, alternative uses of biomass, such as producing bioenergy with or without carbon capture and sequestration can also help to mitigate climate change and may provide greater climate mitigation, lower costs, and/or greater co-benefits in certain contexts.[@woolf2016] This depends on a number of different factors, including soil type, cropland productivity, climate, energy fuel mix, feedstock availability, distance to CO~2~ sinks for carbon capture and storage, energy prices and food prices. For example, bioenergy production may provide a greater climate benefit in regions that are highly dependent on carbon-intensive energy sources and have high soil fertility, whereas biochar is more favorable where low-fertility soils can benefit from its soil-health improvement.[@woolf2016]

It is, therefore, critical to understand where biochar could be the best use of resources from a climate mitigation perspective. Currently, most biochar assessments focus on the technical potential, without mapping out the tradeoffs or identifying optimal pathways based on location. While there are some biochar life-cycle assessments that account for alternative biomass uses, they are highly context-specific and difficult to scale up on[@peters2015; @lefebvre2021]. As such, this project aims to provide a detailed feasibility and tradeoff analysis across four regions (North America, India, China, and Europe) to map where biochar represents the most efficient use of biomass to reduce atmospheric greenhouse gasses (GHGs). These regions represent a diversity of geographic, socio-economic, and agro-ecological conditions for a broad assessment of how constraints, tradeoffs and benefits vary across regions. This work will allow policy-makers and practitioners to make scientifically-informed decisions about which mitigation pathways are best suited for their geographies. It can also help contextualize biochar's mitigation potential by identifying areas that maximize its climate benefits and realistically support its production and application.

# Methods

## Model Architecture

The C-SCAPE (Carbon Spatial Cost and Allocation Pathways Evaluator) model (version 1.0; implemented as the R package BiocharAG) evaluates three biomass utilization pathways: Bioenergy (BES), Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS), and Bioenergy with Biochar Carbon Storage (BEBCS). For each grid cell and technology, the model calculates a discounted cost-benefit balance, expressed as a levelized annual net value per megagram of dry, ash-free feedstock (the net present value annualized with the capital recovery factor; referred to as NPV below). GHG emissions and removals are converted to 100-year CO~2~ equivalents and internalized using an assumed carbon price.

The model was deployed across the coterminous United States, Europe, India, and China. Each region is restricted to its national territory; Europe comprises the countries of geographic Europe within 11°W–40°E and 35–71°N, including Ukraine, Belarus and the part of Türkiye within these bounds, but excluding Russia. All spatial inputs were harmonized to a geographic (WGS84) grid of 0.1° (0.2° for the United States). Area-dependent calculations use cell areas on the ellipsoid, and the biomass collection distances were computed in region-specific equal-area projections (EPSG:5070, EPSG:3035 and Albers equal-area projections for China and India) before being returned to the model grid. The model was implemented in R, using the terra package for spatial analysis [@hijmans2025terra].

The following model description outlines the assumptions, equations and parameters used in the model. The default parameter values are provided in a table at the end of the Methods.

### Biomass Feedstock Sourcing and Logistics

#### Biomass Transport Costs and Emissions

High resolution rasters of available crop residue biomass were derived from the sustainably harvestable crop residues of Karan et al. [@karan2023], which exclude the fraction that must be retained to avoid soil degradation, minus the fraction used as livestock fodder and bedding, estimated for each world region from the stover feed use of @herrero2013. The supply modelled here therefore does not divert residues from these uses. The average transport distance for biomass was calculated from this using focal statistics based on the annual biomass requirement for the conversion facility. The required annual biomass mass ($M_{req}$) is determined by the target thermal capacity, the capacity factor, and the biomass lower heating value (LHV). A spatial focal sum algorithm was applied to aggregate the surrounding biomass over a discrete series of expanding radii (from 5 km up to 500 km). The required collection radius was then calculated via quadratic interpolation between these radial bins. All domains were uniformly projected and resampled to the 0.1 degree ($\sim 10\text{ km}$) equal-area grid prior to executing the focal sum algorithms to ensure methodological consistency. Assuming a circular catchment geometry, the average straight-line collection distance is approximated as two-thirds of the interpolated bounding radius (i.e. assuming homogeneous distribution within the catchment area). The average straight-line distance was multiplied by a tortuosity factor of 1.3 to calculate the effective road transport distance.[@sultana2014] Biomass logistical costs were modeled using a fixed material handling and loading cost and a variable trucking cost applied to the effective road distance. The loading and handling cost is 6.27 \$/Mg (4.59 \$ per dry tonne in 2012 USD, escalated to 2024 USD with the US consumer price index) [@beach2012]. The variable cost of 0.19 \$/Mg/km (0.12 \$/Mg/km for straw and stover in 2006 USD, escalated to 2024 USD with the US consumer price index) is the truck distance-variable cost of @searcy2007, which is expressed per kilometre of one-way distance and includes the empty return trip.

Haulage costs vary with terrain and road access, which the flat per-kilometre rate does not capture. For every candidate plant location and plant size, travel from each field in the collection area to the plant was routed as the least-time path on the global motorised friction surface of @weiss2020, at 30 arc-seconds. Biomass-weighted over the collection area, this gives the travel time and road-path length per kilometre of straight-line distance, and the cumulative climb on the loaded and empty legs. The variable trucking cost was divided into time-based costs (driver wages and benefits, truck finance, insurance; 64%), fuel (24%) and other distance-based costs (repairs, tyres, tolls; 12%), following @atri2024. The time-based share scales with travel time, fuel with road distance and climb, and the remainder with road distance. Climb fuel is the energy to lift the loaded and empty truck over the cumulative ascent of each leg; descents are not credited, because diesel trucks recover little of the energy on downhill grades. Each factor is normalised to a biomass-weighted mean of one within each region, because the regional level of haulage cost is set by the regional haulage cost factor (@tbl-parameters). The factors therefore redistribute haulage cost within a region, from flat, well-connected areas to rugged or poorly connected ones. Biochar is returned to the fields as a backhaul in the feedstock trucks, which run year-round from field-edge storage, so only its loading and handling cost is charged. Field application (spreading and incorporation) is costed per hectare at the biochar application rate [@woolf2016optimal], and the diesel used by the tractor (17.5 L ha^-1^, the median of published estimates for spreading and incorporation [@roberts2010; @pujolpereira2016; @leppakoski2021; @cheng2025]) is counted as an emission. Scope three transportation emissions associated with feedstock procurement were estimated using a heavy-duty diesel transport emissions factor applied to the effective distance, scaled with the fuel factors, and deducted from the net carbon abatement.

#### Fuel Quality

Agricultural crop residues typically have a higher ash content than the wood chips more commonly used in bioenergy combustion. High-ash feedstocks carry significant fouling and slagging risks, requiring additional capital expenditures (CAPEX) and operating expenditure (OPEX), for example through deployment of Circulating Fluidized Bed (CFB) boilers. This fuel quality penalty is modelled, relative to a wood-chip fired bioenergy plant, as an increase in base CAPEX for the combustion technologies (BES and BECCS) of 25% for high-ash feedstocks (ash above 5%) or 10% for medium-ash feedstocks (2–5%), and a reduction in electrical conversion efficiency of 10% or 5% respectively [@dea2026]. O&M costs are not penalised separately: they are charged as a fraction of CAPEX, which already carries the penalty, and straw-fired plants have the same ratio of O&M to investment cost as wood-fired plants [@dea2020]. The fouling, slagging and corrosion risks of high-ash, high-alkali residues are reviewed by @baxter1998, @garcía2017 and @luan2025a.

#### Regional Pricing Structures

Feedstock is priced at the field side (farm gate or road side), in 2024 USD per Mg; haulage from the field to the plant is costed separately (see Biomass Transport Costs and Emissions), so delivered or plant-gate prices are not used. For Europe, China and India the values are costs of collection at the field side, excluding the margins of farmers and intermediaries; for the United States, where no comparable national cost estimate is available, the value is a farm-gate price that includes the grower's payment and profit, so it is somewhat higher than a cost-only estimate would be.

-   **United States:** US\$50 per dry short ton (2011 USD), or 76.9 US\$/Mg in 2024 USD: in the Billion-Ton Update, about 80% of the primary crop residue supply is profitable to collect at a farm-gate price of US\$45 per dry ton and 90% at US\$50 [@perlack2011]. The Billion-Ton prices are uniform across the country because the underlying POLYSYS runs apply a single national price, raised until a large and reliable supply is offered. The farm-gate price comprises the harvest cost and a grower payment that already compensates for the nutrients removed with the residue, so no separate nutrient-replacement charge is added.

-   **Europe:** road-side costs of cereal straw from the S2Biom atlas [@dees2017s2biom], which maps them at NUTS-3 level by activity-based costing, aggregated to country level in three cost classes: €20 per t of dry matter (2012 EUR) for eastern Europe, Poland and the Baltic states; €37.5 for most of central, northern and southern Europe, including France and Spain; and €62.5 for Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. In 2024 USD these are 35.1, 65.8 and 109.7 US\$/Mg. Countries without an S2Biom value are assigned by analogy: Kosovo to the lowest class, like Serbia and Croatia; Cyprus to the middle class, like Greece; and Türkiye and the North African and Middle Eastern countries within the European
 grid to the lowest class, as residue costs there are generally below those of most of Europe.

-   **China:** the field-side cost of collecting corn straw estimated with the StrawFeed supply-chain model for Nongan county, Jilin [@wang2022strawfeed]: raking, baling and loading cost ¥99.6 per t (2019), or 17.7 US\$/Mg in 2024 USD, excluding the ¥72.5 per t of transport to the plant. Like the European and Indian values, this is a cost and excludes the margins of farmers and brokers; power plants in Northeast China pay about ¥300 per t delivered [@wang2022strawfeed], and ¥200–300 per t at the plant gate in other major producing provinces.

-   **India:** paddy straw, which has little value as fodder in the rice–wheat belt of the north-west because of its high silica content and is otherwise burned in the field, is priced at 34 US\$/Mg on a dry basis, the cost of baled straw at the field side estimated for bioenergy supply chains in Haryana [@sokhansanj2023]. The Monte Carlo analysis samples it between about 12 US\$/Mg, reflecting the low value of paddy straw where it is burned [@erenstein2011], and about 50 US\$/Mg, the price of straw traded as fodder [@duncan2020; @lopes2023]. Wheat straw, which is valued as fodder, is not used as a feedstock.

Year-round operation also requires interim storage of residues harvested within a few weeks. Published storage costs vary widely, from about 3 to 42 US\$/Mg (2024 USD): 3–11 for US farm-scale storage [@becerra2022; @brechbill2008; @beach2012], 18 for on-farm and 31 for purpose-built storage in the United Kingdom [@shackley2011], 34 for storage and handling [@kung2013], and about 42 for six months' storage of German straw, where storage is 36.4% of the total supply cost [@karras2024]. We add 15 US\$/Mg for the United States and Europe, sampled from 3 to 42 in the Monte Carlo analysis, and scale it by the regional haulage cost factor for China and India (11 and 10 US\$/Mg), consistent with storage accounting for 20–30% of the delivered cost of paddy straw in India [@ceew2021exsitu].

### Technology Pathways and Thermodynamics

The core thermodynamic engine evaluates three distinct biomass utilization pathways, processing a biomass input of $125\text{ MW}_{\text{th}}$ by default (@tbl-parameters) into varying ratios of exported electrical energy and sequestered carbon.

#### Bioenergy (BES)

The BES pathway represents a traditional, dedicated biomass combustion facility. In this baseline scenario, the feedstock is fully oxidized to maximize electricity exported to the regional grid. Because there is no active carbon capture, the physical carbon embedded in the biomass is returned to the atmosphere.

The technoeconomic parameters for this modern combustion archetype assume a net electrical efficiency of 30% [@dea2026]. Capital expenditures (CAPEX) are specified regionally per kW of net electrical capacity for a 50 MW~e~ wood-fired reference plant (@tbl-parameters), and scale non-linearly with plant capacity via a standard 0.7 scaling factor. The reference CAPEX (2024 USD) is 4,700 \$/kW~e~ for the United States, from the EIA's 50 MW biomass plant [@eia2026], and 4,300 \$/kW~e~ for Europe, from Danish technology data for a 132 MW~th~ straw-fired plant scaled to 50 MW~e~ and adjusted to a wood-fired equivalent by the Danish straw-to-wood cost ratio [@dea2020]. For China and India, where far more biomass plants have been built recently, it is the average installed cost of bioenergy plants commissioned in 2024, 2,200 and 1,900 \$/kW~e~ [@irena2025]; India's regulatory benchmark for rice-straw plants is lower still, about 925 \$/kW~e~ [@cerc2024]. For costing, plant capacity is defined as the thermal input multiplied by a fixed reference net efficiency (`bes_capex_ref_eff`), rather than by the realised efficiency. Equipment cost is therefore set by the size of the boiler and steam cycle, so factors that reduce net output for a given thermal input (the high-ash fuel penalty, efficiency uncertainty, or the parasitic load of carbon capture) reduce revenue without spuriously reducing capital cost. Operations and maintenance (O&M) costs, fixed and variable together, are charged as an annual fraction of total CAPEX (`plant_om_factor`, 4% per year), which is shared by all conversion technologies (BES, BECCS, and the pyrolysis unit and energy block of BEBCS) and the same in every region (see Regional Cost Adjustment). The 4% value is consistent with the EIA reference 50 MW biomass plant (fixed O&M of \$141.5/kW-yr plus variable O&M of \$5.44/MWh, about 3.5% of CAPEX per year at a 70% capacity factor) [@eia2023], with IRENA's range for stoker and fluidized-bed biomass boilers (fixed O&M of 3.2–4.2% of CAPEX per year plus \$3.8–4.7/MWh) [@irena2012], and with Danish technology data for 80 MW~th~ biomass CHP plants (4.4% per year for straw and 4.6% for wood pellets, fixed and variable combined) [@dea2020]. Capital costs are annualized over the plant lifetime at the regional discount rate using the capital recovery factor, so that all costs and revenues are expressed as levelized annual values per megagram of feedstock; because O&M is a constant annual cost, discounting it over the plant lifetime and re-annualizing at the same rate returns the annual value. Total electrical output is derived directly from the biomass lower heating value (LHV, $18.6\text{ GJ/Mg}$ for dry, ash-free feedstock [@phyllis2]) and the plant's capacity factor of 70%, the median levelised capacity factor of US base-load plants (range 65–75%, sampled in the Monte Carlo analysis) [@rubin2012]. Technology data give an availability of 91% for biomass plants [@dea2026], but this accounts only for planned and unplanned outages, not for operation below full output.

When ash recycling is enabled (the default; `ash_recycling`, @tbl-parameters), the bottom and fly ash from BES and BECCS combustion is returned to cropland and credited with its liming value, where soil pH is below the target pH, and its phosphorus fertilizer value, using the same substitution prices and availability factor as biochar (see Biochar Agronomic Valuation). Phosphorus is largely retained in the ash, whereas nitrogen and most of the potassium are volatilized during combustion and are not credited. The default ash liming (calcium carbonate equivalent) and phosphorus contents are set so that, at the default feedstock ash content, the ash and the biochar derived from the same feedstock return equal liming and phosphorus value per megagram of feedstock, so that the pathways differ only in the nitrogen, potassium and soil physical benefits retained by biochar.

#### Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS)

The BECCS pathway augments the standard combustion baseline with a post-combustion carbon capture unit. The addition of this unit imposes a significant parasitic energy penalty, primarily driven by solvent regeneration and CO~2~ compression requirements. Consequently, the net electrical conversion efficiency drops below the BES baseline by an efficiency penalty (default = 8 percentage points).

The capture process is parameterized with a 90% capture efficiency rate. The total volume of captured CO~2~ routed to geological storage is calculated stoichiometrically based on the carbon fraction of the incoming biomass feed (default 48% C [@phyllis2]), converted to CO~2~ mass equivalents using the 44/12 molar ratio. The additional infrastructure (capture unit, CO~2~ compression and flue-gas cleaning) is represented as a premium on total CAPEX relative to a BES plant of the same thermal input (`beccs_capex_premium`, @tbl-parameters). The default premium is based on the IEAGHG techno-economic evaluation of dedicated biomass-fired power plants with post-combustion amine capture, in which capture raised total investment by 38--40% for 75 MW~e~ bubbling and 250 MW~e~ circulating fluidized bed plants [@ieaghg2009]. Because net output fell simultaneously, the corresponding increase in specific capital cost was 114--126% per net kW~e~, consistent with the 45--130% range reported across biomass CCS technologies by @bhave2017. Expressing the premium on a thermal-input basis keeps it independent of the efficiency penalty. Annual O&M is the same fraction of CAPEX as for the other technologies (@tbl-parameters).

### Carbon Transport and Geological Storage

#### Storage Sites and Sink Choice

Geological storage is represented by 45 storage basins across the four regions (onshore saline formations, onshore oil fields suitable for CO~2~-enhanced oil recovery (EOR), and offshore saline formations and depleted fields). Saline storage and EOR are flagged separately, so that petroleum basins with substantial saline storage resource (for example the Ordos, Songliao, Tarim and Junggar basins in China, the Cambay Basin in India and the Permian Basin in the United States) serve as saline sinks as well as EOR sites. They are listed with their locations and types in the model repository. Basin locations and storage types follow the OGCI CO~2~ Storage Resource Catalogue [@ogci2024csrc] and, for the United States, the USGS national assessment of geologic CO~2~ storage resources [@usgs2013co2]; basins added for coverage are located at operating or planned storage projects (for example Porthos, Northern Lights, Greensand, Ravenna CCS, HyNet and Bayou Bend) listed in the Global CCS Institute's CO2RE facilities database [@gccsi2025co2re]. Four transport-and-storage classes are evaluated for every grid cell: pipeline to an onshore saline site; pipeline to an EOR site (only when EOR is allowed, which is not the default); pipeline and ship to an offshore site; and pipeline, including a subsea section, to an offshore site. For each cell and plant size, the model selects the class with the lowest combined transport and storage cost for that plant's CO~2~ flow.

#### Pipeline Routing

Pipeline routes are computed on a grid ten times finer than the model grid (0.02° for the United States, 0.01° elsewhere). Two surfaces are used, one to choose each route and one to cost it, so that the routing can avoid difficult terrain without that avoidance being charged as extra pipeline length. Slope from the 250 m Geomorpho90m dataset [@amatulli2020] is converted, per 250 m pixel, into a construction-cost multiplier $F_{cost}(\theta)$. This multiplier is piecewise linear in slope $\theta$: 1.0 at 0°, 1.05 at 5°, 1.2 at 10°, 1.6 at 17°, 2.3 at 25°, 3.2 at 35° and 4.0 at 45°. The per-pixel values are then averaged to the routing grid, with additive premiums above 2,500 m altitude. <!-- TODO (reference required): terrain and altitude construction-cost multipliers. --> The routing surface adds a planning-risk premium for steep ground, $F_{route} = F_{cost}\,[1 + r_{max}\,\mathrm{logistic}((\theta - 20^\circ)/3^\circ)]$ with $r_{max} = 2$, capped at 25.

Protected areas from the World Database on Protected Areas [@wdpa2026] are tiered. Strictly protected areas (IUCN categories Ia, Ib and II, and natural World Heritage sites) are barriers. Other designated terrestrial protected areas can be crossed at a construction-cost premium of 25% and a routing premium of 100%. Marine protected areas are not applied to the land routing.

Least-cost paths on $F_{route}$ from every cell to the nearest target were computed with terra [@hijmans2025terra]. The resulting route tree was then traced to measure, for each route, its physical length $L$, the line integral of $F_{cost}$ along the route, and the highest point of the route above the source. Pipeline cost is charged on the physical length multiplied by the route-average construction-cost multiplier (the line integral of $F_{cost}$ divided by $L$). No further tortuosity factor is applied. In a robustness test, setting $r_{max}$ between 0 and 2 changed the optimal technology in less than 0.4% of grid cells.

#### Hub-and-Spoke Pipeline Modality

Standard length-invariant TEA cost functions for CO~2~ pipelines adequately model regional networks but underestimate the capital and energy burdens of long-distance transport, which requires intermediate booster compression to overcome frictional pressure drops. Pipeline CAPEX is therefore calculated with a piecewise-linear hub-and-spoke model:

1.  **The Feeder Leg:** Sources build a dedicated feeder pipeline for the first 50 km ($d_{feeder}$), bearing the full CAPEX scaled to their own CO~2~ flow (scaling exponent 0.6). Routes of 50 km or less are dedicated pipelines throughout.

2.  **The Trunk Leg (Base Phase):** Up to 700 km, the source connects to a regional trunkline operating at an efficient scale (3 Mt CO~2~ yr^-1^), paying a share of its CAPEX proportional to its mass flow.

3.  **The Trunk Leg (Booster Phase):** Beyond 700 km, the marginal trunkline cost is doubled ($P_{booster} = 2.0$) to approximate the capital and operating costs of intermediate booster stations.

The trunkline CAPEX share is:

$$CAPEX_{trunk} = m \cdot
\begin{cases}
C_{base} \cdot (L - 50) & \text{if } L \le 700 \\
C_{base} \cdot (700 - 50) + (C_{base} \cdot P_{booster}) \cdot (L - 700) & \text{if } L > 700
\end{cases}$$

Here $L$ is the physical route length (km), $m$ is the route-average construction-cost multiplier (applied to the feeder leg as well), and $C_{base}$ is the unit-length cost of the efficient-scale trunkline, scaled to the source's share of its mass flow. The reference cost is US\$50 million per 100 km for a 1 Mt yr^-1^ pipeline, scaled by the regional CAPEX factor. Annual pipeline O&M is 4% of CAPEX, and pipeline CAPEX is annualized over the 25-year plant lifetime at the regional discount rate. <!-- TODO (reference required): pipeline reference cost, scaling exponent, trunk scale, booster threshold and penalty, O&M fraction. --> Routes that climb require booster pumping to restore the pressure lost in lifting dense-phase CO~2~. Pumps are sized for the lift beyond a 1 MPa design margin, with pump CAPEX following @mccollum2006, and their electricity is charged at the regional electricity price.

#### Maritime Shipping and Subsea Pipelines

CO~2~ destined for offshore sinks is either shipped or carried by pipeline to the sink:

$$C_{ship} = C_{pipeline}(L_{port}) + C_{liquefaction} + C_{terminal} + c_{voyage} \cdot d_{sea}, \qquad C_{subsea} = C_{pipeline}(L_{landfall} + d_{sea})$$

$L_{port}$ and $L_{landfall}$ are the physical lengths of the onshore routes to the port or landfall. $d_{sea}$ is the sea distance from there to the sink, routed on a 0.02–0.04° grid with land impassable. Liquefaction and terminal costs are 20 and 15 US\$ per t CO~2~ (scaled by the regional CAPEX factor), and the voyage costs 0.035 US\$ per t per km. <!-- TODO (reference required): shipping cost parameters. --> For subsea pipelines, the subsea section carries 1.5 times the onshore CAPEX per km.

Every coastal cell is a candidate port or landfall. The land route and the port are chosen together, by a multi-source least-cost search in which each coastal cell starts with its sea leg already priced: 0.7 flat-onshore-pipeline-km per sea km for shipping (the ratio of voyage to trunk-pipeline cost per t km), and 1.5 for subsea pipelines. The route therefore minimizes land and sea cost together rather than land distance alone. Fixed liquefaction and terminal costs do not affect this choice.

Emissions from CO~2~ transport are deducted from the BECCS abatement. For shipping, these are the emissions from liquefaction, loading and the voyage, about 2.5% of the CO~2~ carried over 200 km and about 18% over 12,000 km [@albaroudi2021]. For pipelines, they are the emissions from the booster pumping electricity, at the displaced grid intensity.

#### CO~2~ Injection

CO~2~ injection and storage (injection wells and operations, and measurement, monitoring and verification) is costed separately from both the capture plant and CO~2~ transport, as a fixed cost per megagram of CO~2~ injected, with separate values for onshore and offshore storage sites (`ccs_storage_cost` and `cost_offshore_storage`, @tbl-parameters). The defaults, 10 US\$/t CO~2~ onshore (range 2–33) and 20 US\$/t CO~2~ offshore (range 5–50), follow a recent lifecycle assessment of storage costs from exploration to 50 years of post-closure monitoring. That assessment gives 2–15 US\$/t onshore and 5–31 US\$/t offshore (2024 USD) for reservoirs with open boundary conditions, rising to 5–33 and 8–50 US\$/t for moderate-quality closed reservoirs, and up to 58 and 147 US\$/t for the least favourable closed reservoirs [@gccsi2025]. These ranges are consistent with earlier estimates for European saline aquifers of €2–12/t onshore and €6–20/t offshore [@zep2011]. Because boundary conditions, which depend on the geology, are the main driver of storage cost [@gccsi2025], storage sites are assigned a site-specific cost where the evidence allows. For onshore saline formations in the United States, the cost is the first-year break-even price of the cheapest formation in the sink's state with at least 1 Gt of prospective storage resource (in the basin, where no formation in the state qualifies), from a formation-by-formation model that accounts for pressure build-up and interference [@netl2024scom], escalated from 2023 to 2024 USD. These range from 6.4 US\$/t (Frio Formation, Gulf Coast) to 22.5 and 24.7 US\$/t in the Denver-Julesburg and Appalachian basins. Elsewhere, saline formations are classed as open where they are regionally extensive and well connected (the Utsira and Johansen formations of the northern North Sea, the Dogger aquifer of the Paris Basin and the Miocene sands of the Gulf of Mexico shelf), and as closed where they are compartmentalised (the Buntsandstein of the North German Basin), and take the midpoint of the corresponding range above (open: 8.5 US\$/t onshore and 18 offshore; closed: 19 onshore). Depleted oil and gas fields are not closed aquifers in this sense, because they start below their original pressure; the six depleted fields among the sinks take 16.2 US\$/t, the mean of ZEP's offshore cases with and without re-usable wells (€6 and €10/t in 2009) [@zep2011] escalated to 2024 USD. Sinks without sufficient evidence, including all those in China and India, take the default onshore or offshore values. Site-specific costs are scaled by a common factor sampled from 0.5 to 1.75 in the Monte Carlo analysis (`storage_cost_factor`). The applicable cost follows the sink reached by the route chosen for each grid cell (see Storage Sites and Sink Choice). Because storage costs differ between sinks, the route search starts each sink at its storage cost, expressed as an equivalent length of flat onshore trunk pipeline at 0.05 US\$/t/km (for example, 160 km for 8 US\$/t), so that a farther sink with cheaper storage can be chosen. Injection costs are applied to the mass of CO~2~ captured, in addition to the transport cost and the capture plant's own CAPEX and O&M.

### Bioenergy with Biochar Storage (BEBCS)

Unlike the fully oxidative pathways, the BEBCS pathway relies on thermochemical pyrolysis, producing a solid, recalcitrant carbon matrix (biochar) alongside volatile syngas and bio-oil. The model employs a mass and energy balance approach constrained by elemental conservation of Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen (C, H, O).

The mass yield and elemental composition of the resulting biochar are determined dynamically as a function of the peak pyrolysis temperature ($T_{py}$) and the lignin fraction of the feedstock. Specific yields for non-condensable gases hydrogen ($H_2$), carbon monoxide ($CO$), methane ($CH_4$), and ethylene ($C_2H_4$) are calculated based on temperature-dependent reaction kinetics [@woolf2014]. To close the mass balance, the unaccounted elemental fractions ($U_c, U_h, U_o$) are stoichiometrically partitioned into bio-oil, water ($H_2O$), and carbon dioxide (CO~2~). Bio-oil C and H mass fractions are set at 1.25 and 1.26 times those of the feedstock (e.g. $62.5\%\text{ C}$ and $7.56\%\text{ H}$ for a feedstock with 50% C and 6% H), allowing the final product distribution to be solved analytically [@woolf2014]. The default peak pyrolysis temperature of 500 °C is a modelling assumption representing the medium-temperature class (450–600 °C) of @woolf2021greenhouse and the IPCC inventory guidance [@ipcc2019biochar]; it is sampled ±10% in the Monte Carlo analysis. All yields and energy flows are expressed per megagram of dry, ash-free feedstock, with feedstock ash reporting to the biochar.

The net usable energy flux for the BEBCS pathway is calculated from an explicit energy balance on a consistent higher heating value (HHV) basis. The process heat demand is the HHV of the products (biochar, bio-oil and permanent gases) plus explicit process heat losses, minus the HHV of the feedstock. The HHVs of biochar and bio-oil are calculated via the Dulong formula from their C, H and O fractions, and that of the gas from the heats of combustion of its components. Heat losses comprise conduction through the insulated reactor wall (sized from the plant feed rate and a temperature-dependent solids residence time), the sensible heat of biochar discharged at the pyrolysis temperature, and the latent and sensible heat of the bio-oil vapour, permanent gases and water vapour (feedstock moisture plus reaction water) leaving the heat-recovery system. Because the water vapour term includes the latent heat of all water leaving the process, expressing both feedstock and products on an HHV basis avoids double-counting that latent heat. Process heat is supplied by combusting the syngas and bio-oil vapours in a process heater (80% efficiency, HHV basis), and the plant's parasitic electricity demand (0.07 GJ~e~ per Mg feed) is met from the same fuel [@woolf2014]. If the syngas and bio-oil are insufficient to meet these loads, a portion of the biochar is oxidized to close the energy balance, proportionally reducing the final carbon sequestration yield. The remaining fuel, converted to a lower heating value basis, is used to generate electricity in a dedicated power block (35% net electrical efficiency, LHV basis [@woolf2014]), whose capital cost is sized on its actual fuel input using the same reference-plant scaling as the combustion pathways.

The pyrolysis unit CAPEX is 335 US\$ per Mg yr^-1^ of feed capacity in the United States (2024 USD), for the feed of a 50 MW~e~ reference plant, from NREL's nth-plant estimate for a 2,000 dry t day^-1^ slow pyrolysis plant [@yadav2026] scaled to the reference size with an exponent of 0.7. The power block, which burns the pyrolysis vapours and gases and raises steam for a condensing turbine, costs 3,250 US\$/kW~e~ in the United States. This lies between the cost of a steam cycle alone in NREL's pyrolysis designs, about 2,650 US\$/kW~e~ [@dutta2015], and that of a complete 50 MW biomass power plant, which also includes solid-fuel handling (4,700 US\$/kW~e~; @eia2026). Both costs are scaled to other regions by the capital cost location factor (see Regional Cost Adjustment).

#### Biochar Permanence

The Bioenergy with Biochar Storage (BEBCS) pathway diverts a fraction of the original biomass carbon into a recalcitrant solid matrix. While physical disposal methods such as the landfilling of biochar represent a highly effective method to provide highly stable carbon storage, this framework strictly evaluates soil application to quantify the cascading agronomic co-benefits and regional substitution values. Consequently, the carbon retention within the soil matrix is finite and must be modeled dynamically based on localized biogeochemical conditions.

##### Biochar Carbon Permanence ($F_{perm}$)

To accurately quantify the net carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of the BEBCS pathway, the model calculates the permanent carbon fraction ($F_{perm}$) that remains stabilized in the soil after a 100-year time horizon. This fraction is derived using the multi-pool decay methodology established by @woolf2021greenhouse.

The baseline degradation rates of the biochar's labile and recalcitrant carbon pools are fitted to either the peak pyrolysis temperature ($T_{py}$) or the molar Hydrogen-to-Organic-Carbon (H:C) ratio of the final char. The model uses the H:C ratio, derived from the temperature-dependent biochar composition, so that biochar yield and permanence respond jointly to $T_{py}$. Because microbial and chemical degradation kinetics are highly temperature-dependent, these reference decay rates are spatially adjusted to match the localized mean annual soil temperature using a $Q_{10}$ temperature sensitivity function. To optimize spatial computational efficiency across the high-resolution rasters, the thermodynamic module utilizes bilinear interpolation over a pre-calculated matrix of $F_{perm}$ values bounded by soil temperatures ($-55^\circ\text{C}$ to $40^\circ\text{C}$) and H:C ratios ($0.0$ to $0.7$).

Total carbon sequestered per megagram of feedstock is therefore modeled as:

$$C_{seq} = Yield_{bc} \cdot C_{content} \cdot F_{perm} \cdot \left(\frac{44}{12}\right)$$

where $Yield_{bc}$ is the mass fraction of biochar produced, $C_{content}$ is the carbon mass fraction of the biochar, and the $44/12$ ratio converts the elemental carbon to CO~2~ mass equivalents.

##### Soil N~2~O Emission Reduction

Biochar additions to soil can suppress nitrous oxide (N~2~O) emissions from nitrogen fertilizer. From field trials with biochar additions exceeding 10 Mg C ha^-1^, @woolf2021greenhouse estimated a 23% reduction in N~2~O emissions (95% confidence interval 5--41%). The model credits this fractional reduction ($R_{N_2O}$) against direct fertilizer-induced N~2~O emissions on land receiving biochar at that application rate ($A_{bc}$), where direct emissions are the regional mineral N application rate ($N_{app}$) multiplied by the IPCC Tier 1 emission factor ($EF_1$) [@ipcc2019]. Because significant effects have only been demonstrated in the first year after application [@woolf2021greenhouse], the reduction is assumed to persist for a short period ($t_{N_2O}$), with a long upper tail in the Monte Carlo analysis to reflect the uncertainty. The credit per megagram of feedstock is:

$$A_{N_2O} = \frac{N_{app} \cdot EF_1 \cdot R_{N_2O} \cdot t_{N_2O} \cdot C_{bc}}{A_{bc}} \cdot \frac{44}{28} \cdot GWP_{N_2O} \cdot 10^{-3}$$

where $C_{bc}$ is the biochar carbon yield (Mg C per Mg feedstock), $GWP_{N_2O}$ is the 100-year global warming potential of N~2~O [@forster2021], and parameter values are given in @tbl-parameters. Because the effect is short-lived and spread over the large area to which biochar is applied, this credit is small relative to the carbon stored in the biochar.

#### Biochar Agronomic Valuation

Previous spatial models frequently value biochar using a static, exogenous global market price. To better reflect real-world agricultural economics, C-SCAPE endogenously determines the economic credit of biochar through a mechanistic substitution valuation. This assumes that the shadow price of biochar is equal to the cost of the conventional agricultural inputs it offsets:

$$Value_{ag} = Value_{lime} + Value_{nutrients} + Value_{physical}$$

1.  **Liming Equivalence (**$Value_{lime}$): The model spatially evaluates the native soil pH against a neutral agricultural target (pH 6.5). If the soil is acidic, the biochar's Calcium Carbonate Equivalent (CCE, default 15%) is credited against the cost of the agricultural lime it displaces. Because substitution also avoids hauling and spreading the lime, this cost includes transport and application. It is the median of published values, each converted to a calcium carbonate equivalent of 100% and escalated to 2024 US dollars: 59 \$/Mg, ranging from 31 \$/Mg for lime delivered to Brazilian pastures, excluding spreading [@latawiec2019], through 52 \$/Mg in Oklahoma [@mills2020lime] and 59–110 \$/Mg near to and far from a quarry in Oklahoma [@cho2020lime], to 85 \$/Mg spread in North Carolina [@woods2026]. The range is sampled in the Monte Carlo analysis. If the regional soil is already alkaline, the liming value is strictly zero.
2.  **Nutrient Substitution (**$Value_{nutrients}$): The available nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) fractions within the biochar are credited against prevailing regional fertilizer costs. Nutrients are valued at the world market prices of standard commercial fertilizers: urea for N (1.06 US\$/kg N), triple superphosphate for P (1.27 US\$/kg P~2~O~5~) and potassium chloride for K (0.86 US\$/kg K~2~O). These are averages of the World Bank's annual prices for 2021–2025, each escalated to 2024 USD [@worldbank2026pinksheet]. The same prices are used in every region: retail subsidies (as in India) and export controls (as in China) move farm-gate prices away from world prices, but they transfer value rather than change the economic value of the fertilizer displaced. Elemental P and K contents are converted to their oxide equivalents (×2.29 for P~2~O~5~ and ×1.20 for K~2~O) before pricing, and each nutrient is credited at its first-year plant availability (N 10%, P 50%, K 80%; @tbl-parameters).
3.  **Physical/CEC Improvements (**$Value_{physical}$): Biochar raises the cation exchange capacity (CEC) of soils, improving their retention and supply of nutrients and water; the effect is largest in sandy or degraded soils. Unlike liming, this benefit is valued as a yield increment rather than as a substitute input. Agricultural lime is an equivalent substitute for biochar (or ash) as a pH amendment, so the liming benefit is credited at the cost of the lime it displaces. Fertilizer, however, is not a substitute for CEC but a complementary input: a soil with low CEC cannot retain and supply nutrients effectively and responds poorly to fertilizer, so raising its CEC lifts the whole fertilizer response curve, including the economically optimal application rate. The annual yield benefit is 21.1 US\$ per Mg of biochar carbon in soils with a CEC of 5 cmol/kg or less. It is derived from the mean crop-yield benefit of 30 US\$/Mg C per year in @woolf2016optimal (average 2008–2013 prices), of which about half is attributable to CEC and half to pH (the latter credited separately as the liming value), escalated to 2024 USD. The benefit falls linearly with increasing CEC to zero at 30 cmol/kg; this linear scaling is a heuristic.

Liming and nutrient values are one-off credits per megagram of biochar applied. The CEC of biochar increases rather than declines as it ages in soil, through oxidation and functionalization of its surfaces, so the physical benefit is treated as persisting for as long as the biochar carbon remains. Its present value is the annual benefit divided by the sum of the regional discount rate and the decay rate of biochar carbon, the latter being the mean rate implied by the 100-year permanence factor ($k = -\ln F_{perm}/100$; see Biochar Permanence).

### Baseline energy system and offsets

To robustly account for the climate mitigation benefit of bioenergy generation, the framework evaluates greenhouse gas offsets using a consequential Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) boundary. Total carbon abatement is calculated distinctively for each technology pathway, balancing active sequestration, grid displacement credits, and Scope 3 supply chain emissions.

##### Net Carbon Abatement Balances

The net carbon abatement for each grid cell is defined as the sum of physical carbon sequestered and emissions displaced, minus the transportation emissions penalty:

-   **BES:** Abatement relies entirely on the displacement of grid emissions, minus the Scope 3 emissions associated with diesel trucking of the biomass feedstock.
-   **BECCS:** Abatement includes the physical CO~2~ captured and injected into the geological sink (assuming a 90% capture rate) plus the grid displacement credit. However, because the parasitic energy load of the capture process reduces the net electrical efficiency, the total energy exported and thus the resulting grid displacement credit is proportionally lower for BECCS than for pure BES.
-   **BEBCS:** Abatement combines the grid displacement credit with the permanent CO~2~ equivalent of the biochar carbon retained in the soil ($F_{perm}$) and the avoided soil N~2~O emissions ($A_{N_2O}$), minus the diesel emissions of biochar field application.

For BECCS, the emissions of CO~2~ transport are also deducted (see Maritime Shipping). The residue removal counterfactual below applies to all pathways.

For all pathways, Scope 3 feedstock transport emissions are modeled dynamically by applying a heavy-duty diesel transport emissions factor ($0.0001\text{ Mg CO}_2\text{e}$ per $\text{Mg}\cdot\text{km}$) to the effective biomass collection distance.

#### Residue Removal Counterfactual

Removing crop residues for energy has two further effects on greenhouse gas balances that are common to all pathways, relative to a counterfactual in which residues remain in the field. First, retained residues add to soil organic carbon (SOC); residue retention increases SOC stocks by around 10% relative to removal [@bolinder2020]. Retained residues also add nitrogen to the soil and increase soil N~2~O emissions. Process-based simulations across more than 400 million hectares of cropland found that, through to 2100, the SOC gain and the N~2~O increase from retaining more residue approximately cancel almost everywhere, the Brazilian Cerrado being the main exception [@mcclelland2025]. The net soil GHG penalty of removal ($P_{soil}$, Mg CO~2~e per Mg feed) is therefore set to zero by default, and retained as a parameter for sensitivity analysis (@tbl-parameters). A penalty that counted the forgone SOC alone, without the offsetting N~2~O, would be about 0.19 Mg CO~2~e per Mg feed. Second, in regions where residues are commonly burned in the field, removal avoids the non-CO~2~ emissions from open burning (CO~2~ from burning is biogenic and is not counted). These are estimated with the IPCC Tier 1 emission factors for methane and nitrous oxide from burning agricultural residues and the associated combustion factor [@ipcc2006], applied to the share of the available residue in each grid cell that would otherwise be burned ($f_{burn}$). The burnt mass is estimated from the burnt share of cereal residue production in each 0.5° cell (2017–2021 mean) of a global cereal residue dataset that combines satellite fire observations with residue production [@smerald2023], multiplied by the cereal field residue production underlying the residue supply [@karan2023]; $f_{burn}$ is this mass divided by the available residue, both averaged to the model grid, and capped at 1. Using the burnt share rather than the burnt mass keeps the different residue totals of the two datasets out of the ratio. Burning of non-cereal residues, such as sugarcane trash, is not counted, and satellite fire products under-detect small field fires, so the estimate is conservative; a multiplier sampled from 0.5 to 1.5 represents this uncertainty in the Monte Carlo analysis. The biomass-weighted mean of $f_{burn}$ is 2% in the United States, 6% in Europe, 3% in China and 14% in India, and burning is concentrated in Punjab and Haryana in India, Ukraine and the Balkans in Europe, and north-eastern China:

$$A_{residue} = f_{burn} \cdot CF \cdot \left(EF_{CH_4} \cdot GWP_{CH_4} + EF_{N_2O} \cdot GWP_{N_2O}\right) \cdot 10^{-3} - P_{soil}$$

where $CF$ is the combustion factor, $EF$ the emission factors (g kg^-1^ dry matter), and $GWP$ the 100-year global warming potentials [@forster2021]; parameter values are given in @tbl-parameters. Because the same term applies to every pathway, it does not change which technology is preferred in a grid cell, but it changes the absolute net abatement and therefore shifts the marginal abatement cost curves.

#### Grid Displacement

The carbon intensity of the electricity (or heat) displaced by bioenergy output depends on how far the energy system has decarbonized, which in turn depends on the carbon price. Because the carbon price $P$ is an exogenous input to the analysis, the displaced marginal emission factor (MEF) is modeled as a continuous function of $P$, so that the model does not combine a high carbon price with a fossil-dominated grid margin. Each grid cell's empirical build margin at today's explicit carbon price is used as an anchor and scaled by a regional price-response curve calibrated to integrated assessment scenarios.

**Empirical anchor.** New bioenergy capacity is assumed to displace the technology mix currently expanding on each grid. Using monthly national and US state electricity generation data [@ember2025], the sources with positive net generation growth ($\Delta G_i > 0$) between 2019 and 2024 are identified, and the build-margin intensity is their growth-weighted mean:

$$MEF_{emp} = \frac{\sum_i \Delta G_{i} \cdot CI_{i}}{\sum_i \Delta G_{i}}$$

where $CI_i$ is the IPCC median life-cycle greenhouse gas intensity of source $i$ [@schlomer2014]: coal (820 g CO~2~e/kWh), natural gas (490), solar (48), geothermal (38), hydro (24), nuclear (12) and wind (11.5). Bioenergy generation is assigned zero intensity, because bioenergy emissions are accounted for explicitly in the model; growth in bioenergy generation still counts in the denominator. Where no growth data are available, the average grid intensity is used. The resulting anchors are 378 g CO~2~e/kWh for China and 574 for India, with medians over biomass-producing grid cells of 341 for the United States (state level) and 38 for Europe (country level).

**Price-response curve.** The decline of the displaced intensity with carbon price follows a Hill (log-logistic) curve,

$$MEF(P) = MEF_{min} + \left(MEF_{emp} - MEF_{min}\right) \frac{H(P)}{H(P_{now})}, \qquad H(P) = \frac{1}{1 + (P/P_{50})^{k}}$$

where $P_{now}$ is the region's current explicit carbon price on power-sector emissions (@tbl-parameters: the EU Emissions Trading System and China's national emissions trading scheme; no national price in the United States or India), so that the curve passes through each cell's empirical anchor at today's price. The scenario carbon price is thus interpreted as an explicit price: for a given explicit price, the curve gives the intensity of the electricity that new bioenergy capacity would displace, with today's non-price policies embedded in the empirical anchor. Prices below today's level imply a more carbon-intensive margin than observed, capped at the intensity of coal. $MEF_{min}$ = 20 g CO~2~e/kWh is the residual life-cycle intensity of a decarbonized grid [@pehl2017]. The midpoint price $P_{50}$ and steepness $k$ were fitted for each region to the NGFS Phase 5 scenarios (seven scenarios; GCAM 6.0 and MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM 2.0) [@ngfs2026], by robust least squares with equal model weights. GCAM reports the United States, India and the European Union as native regions. For MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM, whose native regions are larger aggregates, the NGFS country-level downscaled results for the United States, India and the EU-27 were used, with coal and gas generation divided into unabated and CCS shares according to the parent region. For each model, the fleet-average intensity of electricity generation at each five-year step was normalized by that model's own low-price value, so that only the shape of the decline, and not its level, is transferred to the empirical anchors. The fleet average was used rather than the models' build margin because, in these scenarios, new capacity is already predominantly renewable at zero carbon price, leaving the build margin with little price response; the fleet average tracks the decarbonization of the system that a baseload plant displaces over its lifetime. A two-stage variant (coal-to-gas switching, then decarbonization) was selected by the Akaike information criterion for Europe only; single-stage curves were imposed for China and India, where coal-to-gas switching is limited by gas availability. The fitted midpoints are $P_{50}$ = 103 US\$/t CO~2~ for the United States, 53 for China and 44 for India, and 45 and 138 US\$/t for the two stages in Europe (2024 USD). REMIND-MAgPIE was excluded from the fit because its grid decarbonizes over time even at low carbon prices, so that its price response could not be separated from its time trend. Parameter uncertainty is represented by 1,000 bootstrap draws over models and scenarios, which are sampled in the Monte Carlo analysis. Because the same carbon price values removals and emissions, the displaced intensity declines as the removal price rises. In the heat sensitivity scenario (see Uncertainty and Sensitivity Analyses), heat is credited separately against fossil boiler heat or a grid heat pump.

### Regional Cost Adjustment

The combustion plant CAPEX of BES and BECCS is specified for each region directly (see Bioenergy). Other capital costs (pyrolysis plants, the BEBCS power block, pipelines, liquefaction and port terminals) are specified for a base location and scaled by a regional capital cost location factor, so that the relative cost of technologies is consistent within each region. O&M is charged at the same fraction of CAPEX in every region, so its absolute level follows regional CAPEX. The fraction does not fall where labour is cheaper: India's regulated O&M allowance for biomass plants is 7.8% of the regulated CAPEX per year [@cerc2024], compared with about 4% in the United States and Europe [@eia2026; @dea2020]. Biomass haulage costs are scaled by a regional road-freight cost factor (@tbl-parameters). <!-- TODO (reference required): CAPEX multipliers. --> 

### Spatial Input Data

Crop residue availability is the sustainably harvestable residue of @karan2023 (net of residues retained for soil protection), minus the regional fraction used as livestock fodder and bedding [@herrero2013]. Feedstock composition is representative of cereal straws, corn stover and rice straw in the Phyllis2 database [@phyllis2]: 48% carbon and a lower heating value of 18.6 GJ/Mg on a dry, ash-free basis, with ash 5% of dry mass in the United States and Europe, where wheat straw and corn stover predominate, and 15% in China and India, where rice straw makes up a large share. Soil pH and cation exchange capacity (0–5 cm) are from SoilGrids 2.0 [@poggio2021] and mean annual soil temperature (0–5 cm) from the global soil bioclimatic maps of @lembrechts2022. Electricity is valued at the wholesale price a generator receives, rather than at retail tariffs, whose regional differences largely reflect taxes, network charges and cross-subsidies. Prices are averages over 2024–2025, excluding the anomalous prices of the 2022 European gas crisis and its aftermath in 2023. For the United States, each state takes the price at the wholesale trading hub of the market that serves most of it (11 hubs) [@eia2026steo]. For Europe, prices are national day-ahead market prices [@ember2026price], with those of Türkiye [@epias2026] and Ukraine [@marketoperator2026] from their market operators; small markets without published prices take a neighbouring market's price. Belarus, which has no wholesale market, takes its industrial tariff [@climatescope2021] multiplied by the ratio of wholesale to industrial prices in the United States (median across states in 2024, 0.42) [@eia2026steo; @eia2025epa]. For China, the price is the provincial benchmark on-grid tariff for coal-fired power [@ndrc2019], which is also the reference price for renewable generators, excluding value-added tax. For India, it is the average price on the day-ahead market of the Indian Energy Exchange in 2024-25 [@cerc2025stm], a single national value because the market rarely separates into regional prices. Each year's price is converted at that year's average exchange rate [@worldbank2026fx] and escalated to 2024 US dollars. The biomass-weighted mean prices are 40 \$/MWh for the United States, 96 for Europe, 47 for China and 49 for India. Grid carbon intensities are described under Grid Displacement.

### Economic Evaluation and Technology Selection

For each grid cell and technology, the net value per megagram of feedstock is the sum of revenues (electricity sales, the carbon price multiplied by the net abatement, and the agronomic value of biochar or ash) minus costs. The costs are annualized CAPEX, O&M, feedstock and haulage, and, for BECCS, CO~2~ transport and storage. CAPEX is annualized with the capital recovery factor at the regional discount rate over the technology lifetime (25 years for BES and BECCS [@dea2026]; 20 years for the pyrolysis unit and 25 years for its power block [@woolf2016optimal]). The regional discount rates are real, after-tax costs of capital for bioenergy projects: 5.6% for the United States, 6.8% for Europe, 6.2% for China and 7.1% for India. They are the nominal costs of capital in US dollars projected for 2030 by @hatton2025, converted to real terms with an expected inflation rate of 2.5%. We use after-tax rates, as is usual in techno-economic assessment. Grossing them up to pre-tax rates at statutory corporate tax rates [@enache2024] would add 3–4 percentage points, but would overstate the effective tax burden, which depreciation allowances reduce. Real rates are required because all cash flows, including the carbon price, are expressed in constant 2024 US dollars. All costs are in 2024 US dollars: values from other years are escalated with the US consumer price index (CPI-U), and values in other currencies are converted at the average exchange rate of the source year before escalation. The plant has a thermal input of 125 MW~th~ by default, and the preferred technology in each cell is the one with the highest net value. Because the displaced grid intensity falls as the carbon price rises (see Grid Displacement), net abatement, and hence net value, is not linear in the carbon price. We therefore evaluate the model on a grid of carbon prices (0–250 US\$/t CO~2~ in steps of 5 US\$/t, and 275–500 US\$/t in steps of 25 US\$/t) and interpolate abatement linearly between grid points; net value is the carbon-price-independent part plus the carbon price multiplied by the interpolated abatement. The break-even carbon price of a technology is the lowest carbon price at which its net value becomes non-negative. Marginal abatement cost curves assign each grid cell, at each carbon price, to the technology with the highest net value if that value is non-negative, and sum the biomass, area and abatement of the assigned cells.

### Uncertainty and Sensitivity Analyses

Parameter uncertainty was propagated by Monte Carlo simulation, with 5,000 draws per region. Each parameter with an uncertainty range was sampled from a PERT or uniform distribution, with the central values, distributions and bounds listed in Table S1 of the Supplementary Information, and correlated parameters were sampled jointly through a Gaussian copula. The uncertainty of the grid displacement curve was represented by sampling one of its 1,000 bootstrap draws in each iteration. The drivers of each technology's net value were identified by fitting gradient-boosted regression trees [XGBoost; @chen2016xgboost] to the Monte Carlo results and computing SHAP values [@lundberg2017]. The same method was applied across grid cells, to the choice of preferred technology, to identify its spatial drivers. A full factorial analysis evaluated 720 scenarios: four regions, carbon prices of 0–200 US\$/t CO~2~, real discount rates of 2%, 5% and 10%, plant sizes of 50, 150 and 250 MW~th~, with and without CO~2~-EOR, and with and without early adoption. Under early adoption, each plant builds a dedicated pipeline over the full distance to the sink instead of sharing a trunkline.

A heat sensitivity scenario tests BEBCS selling heat instead of electricity. The surplus pyrolysis vapours and gases are burned in a heat-only block (80% efficiency, 400 US\$/kW~th~, 25-year life) rather than the power block. Heat is valued at the no-carbon cost of the heat it displaces, the fuel price divided by boiler efficiency: 17 US\$/MWh for industrial gas in the United States, 41 for gas in Europe, 23 for coal in China and 15 for coal in India (@tbl-parameters). The displaced emissions are those of the cleaner of a fossil boiler (0.25 t CO~2~/MWh for gas and 0.45 for coal, life cycle) and a heat pump supplied by the grid at the displaced grid intensity MEF(P) with a seasonal coefficient of performance of 3, so that displaced heat decarbonizes with the grid as the carbon price rises. BES and BECCS are unchanged. The scenario assumes that the plant sells all its heat, which requires a year-round heat demand (for example an industrial process or a district heating network) at the plant. Because the model does not map heat demand, the scenario is reported cell by cell, as the outcome where such demand exists, and is not aggregated to regional totals.

### Model Parameters and Data Sources

To ensure full reproducibility and transparency, the operational, financial, and biophysical parameters utilized within the C-SCAPE framework are tabulated below. Parameters are classified by their spatial resolution: **Scalar** values are held constant globally; **Regional** values act as constants but are overridden based on the macro-economic domain (e.g., India, China, Europe, US); and **Spatial** values are resolved dynamically at the grid-cell level using high-resolution raster datasets.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-parameters
#| tbl-cap: "Operational, financial, and biophysical parameters of the C-SCAPE model."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(gt)
library(dplyr)

raw_params <- read.csv("../BiocharAG/inst/extdata/parameters.csv", check.names = FALSE, na.strings = "")

# Filter out rows that shouldn't be displayed
# Exclude Constants, Control Flags, and some spatial metrics
display_df <- raw_params |>
  filter(!(category %in% c("Constants", "Control Flags"))) |>
  filter(!(name %in% c("avg_dist", "collection_radius", "dist_offshore", "dist_onshore", "dist_sink_km", "dist_sink_saline_km", "feedstock_cost", "tortuosity", "plant_sizes_mw_th", "flat_ci_tCO2_GJ", "rebound"))) |>
  select(
    Category = category,
    Parameter = name,
    Description = description,
    USA = US,
    Europe = Europe,
    China = China,
    India = India,
    Units = units
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert NA to Spatially explicit for regional columns
    USA = ifelse(is.na(USA), "Spatially explicit", USA),
    Europe = ifelse(is.na(Europe), "Spatially explicit", Europe),
    China = ifelse(is.na(China), "Spatially explicit", China),
    India = ifelse(is.na(India), "Spatially explicit", India),
    # Add backticks to Parameter names for markdown formatting
    Parameter = paste0("`", Parameter, "`")
  ) |>
  # Arrange by Category
  arrange(Category)

# Identify rows where all regional values are identical
is_uniform <- with(display_df, !is.na(USA) & USA == Europe & Europe == China & China == India & USA != "Spatially explicit")

display_df$Europe[is_uniform] <- ""
display_df$China[is_uniform] <- ""
display_df$India[is_uniform] <- ""

gt(display_df, groupname_col = "Category") |>
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Value",
    columns = c(USA, Europe, China, India)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Parameter = "Parameter",
    Description = "Description",
    USA = "USA/Default",
    Europe = "Europe",
    China = "China",
    India = "India",
    Units = "Units"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    Parameter ~ pct(18),
    Description ~ pct(24),
    USA ~ pct(12),
    Europe ~ pct(10),
    China ~ pct(10),
    India ~ pct(10),
    Units ~ pct(16)
  ) |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = c(Category, Parameter, Description, USA, Europe, China, India, Units)) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(9),
    data_row.padding = px(2),
    row_group.font.weight = "bold",
    latex.use_longtable = TRUE,
    latex.header_repeat = TRUE
  )
```

# Results

## Capital Intensive Pathways are Highly Sensitive to Discount Rates and Carbon Prices

Figures [fig-evap-usa](#fig-evap-usa) to [fig-evap-china](#fig-evap-china) illustrate the core vulnerability of CDR pathways to capital lock-out. Because both BECCS (heavy upfront infrastructure) and BEBCS (deferred agronomic value) are highly sensitive to the cost of capital, high discount rates act as a strong barrier to adoption, forcing a retreat to traditional Bioenergy (BES) without high carbon prices. For example, in the USA, at a 2% social discount rate and a \$30/t carbon price, BEBCS covers a large extent of the US Midwest and South, with BECCS only being viable close to CO~2~ sinks. However, stepping up to the 8% market baseline eliminates BEBCS's advantage, replacing it with almost entirely with BES. The value of biochar relies heavily on liming and nutrient substitution benefits that are amortized over a 10-year agronomic impact duration. At an 8% or 15% discount rate, the present value of those future soil benefits is diminished, rendering the upfront thermal penalties of pyrolysis economically unviable at low carbon prices. At a 2% discount rate and intermediate carbon price (around \$100/t), BECCS is nearly universal across the US. At 15%, the BECCS dominance is fractured, with BES reclaiming the geographic margins (e.g., the Northeast and far West), and BEBCS remaining only in localized pockets where soil conditions make it particularly attractive. This occurs because, when capital is expensive, the penalty for long-distance pipelines becomes insurmountable until carbon prices reach the \$150/t range. By the time the carbon price reaches \$150/t, the maps become almost entirely red across all discount rates. At this pricing level, the high CDR capture efficiency overwhelms the high cost of capital, making BECCS the most economically attractive option.

## Biochar provides a mid-price transition technology option and a long term solution for specific agro-ecological zones

Figure [fig-evap-china](#fig-evap-china) provides a counterpoint to the US results. It shows how soils with strong production constraints that can be alleviated by biochar can create a persistent competitive advantage for biochar, particularly when combined with large distances to CO~2~ storage sites. BEBCS performs a central role as a transition technology that peaks at intermediate carbon prices that are high enough to make its carbon sequestration competitive with BES, but not so high that the more efficient CDR of BECCS per unit biomass outcompetes it (Figures [fig-MACC-eur](#fig-MACC-eur), [fig-MACC-india](#fig-MACC-india), and [fig-MACC-china](#fig-MACC-china)). Nonetheless, while BECCS ultimately becomes the optimal technology across the entire US spatial domain at high carbon prices, BEBCS remains the most viable pathway in southern China across almost all price and discount rate scenarios. This demonstrates that BEBCS is not merely a transition technology, but the optimal long-term pathway for specific agro-ecological zones. In Southern China, characterized by highly weathered, acidic soils, the biochar's liming and nutrient use efficiency benefits provide a substantial economic credit that buffers against high processing costs. The model scales physical yield efficiency gains inversely to the soil's native Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC), thus granting severe CEC deficits higher premiums. This is confirmed by the SHAP analysis (Figure [fig-shap-dominant](#fig-shap-dominant)), which identifies soil CEC as the dominant spatial driver in this region.

## Regional Policies Hinder Biochar Competitiveness

In India, on the other hand, the mid carbon price advantage of BEBCS is almost entirely eliminated, with BECCS eventually covering most of the map at high carbon prices. Here, fertilizer subsidies hamper BEBCS's economic viability. Because BEBCS economics relies on improved nutrient use efficiency and lower fertilizer inputs per unit crop yield, cheap subsidized synthetic fertilizers erode biochar's nutrient substitution value. Despite this, Biochar maintains a strong foothold in the regions in the North East, North West, and central Eastern coastal regions of India where low soil CEC is a major constraint to crop production.

## Regional Energy prices and Carbon Intensity provide a critical constraint on the optimal CDR pathways

At lower carbon prices The optimal technology in Europe is almost universally BES, driven by high energy prices as the dominant driver across Europe. At \$30 / t CO~2~, the revenue from maximized power generation in BES outweighs the incentive to capture and sequester carbon, rendering the capital expenditure for BECCS and BEBCS unviable across all discount rates. As carbon prices increase, BECCS begins to dominate across central and northern Europe. BEBCS gains a strong advantage in Southern Europe, and Eastern Scandinavia where various combinations of large distances to CO~2~ sinks, already-low carbon intensity of the energy systems, and infertile soils make it more competitive. As in China, we see BEBCS maintain its advantage in these regions, even at very high carbon prices.

## Biochar with heat recovery where year-round heat demand exists

Where a plant can sell its heat year-round, heat recovery raises the net value of BEBCS in every region (@fig-heat-delta-map, @fig-heat-delta). At a carbon price of 100 US\$/t CO~2~, the median gain per megagram of biomass is 36 US\$ in the United States, 41 US\$ in Europe (interquartile range across cells 21–62 US\$, largest in the Nordic countries, France and Iberia, where electricity is cheap), 26 US\$ in China and 7 US\$ in India, and it varies little with the carbon price. Heat abates slightly less than electricity per megagram of biomass, because each unit of heat displaces less CO~2~ than a unit of electricity, especially as the grid decarbonizes. The gain is therefore economic rather than climatic: heat earns more than electricity from the same fuel, at a much lower capital cost. Where heat demand exists, heat recovery keeps BEBCS the preferred option at high carbon prices in much of the United States and western and northern Europe, where BECCS would otherwise prevail (@fig-heat-optimal). In China and India, where the displaced heat comes from cheap coal, BECCS remains preferred at 200 US\$/t CO~2~. Because suitable heat demand is limited in most residue-producing areas, these results indicate where biochar plants would benefit from co-location with heat users, rather than an expansion of BEBCS across the region.

## Competing Uses of Crop Residues

The analysis values crop residues against two counterfactuals: retention in the field, whose net soil GHG effect is close to zero [@mcclelland2025], and open burning, whose avoided CH~4~ and N~2~O emissions are credited. A third use, livestock fodder and bedding, is excluded from the supply: the sustainably harvestable residue of @karan2023, which is net of the fraction that must be retained to avoid soil degradation, is reduced by the fraction already used as fodder and bedding [@herrero2013]. This matters most in India, where cereal straws are a major source of fodder, whereas rice straw in the north-western rice–wheat belt is largely burned. Where the fodder fraction is underestimated locally, diverting residues would displace feed that must be replaced from other sources, with associated emissions, land use and costs; the net abatement estimated here is therefore most robust where residues would otherwise be burned or left in the field.

# Conclusion

The deployment of biomass for climate change mitigation cannot be guided by a single universal pathway. Our spatial analysis demonstrates that the economic viability of BES, BECCS, and BEBCS is dictated by a complex interplay of localized biophysical constraints and regional market dynamics.

While BECCS offers the highest theoretical carbon removal potential, its heavy infrastructure requirements and sensitivity to the cost of capital create significant barriers to entry, particularly where biomass is located far from suitable geological sinks. In contrast, biochar (BEBCS) circumvents these transport constraints and establishes a resilient economic niche in regions with degraded, low-CEC soils, where its agronomic co-benefits—such as liming equivalence and nutrient substitution—offset its lower electrical conversion efficiencies. Southern China exemplifies this dynamic, demonstrating that BEBCS is a robust, long-term mitigation strategy for specific agro-ecological zones rather than merely a transition technology.

Furthermore, baseline energy markets shape optimal pathways. In Europe, high wholesale electricity prices establish BES as the dominant pathway at low carbon prices.

Realizing the climate mitigation potential of global biomass requires moving beyond blanket technological mandates. Policymakers must adopt spatially explicit strategies that target BECCS deployment near geological sinks, incentivize BEBCS in agro-ecological zones suffering from soil degradation, and recognize the enduring role of BES in displacing highly carbon-intensive fossil grids.
